title: Chunk hashing for file sync with a benchmark
name: Chunk indexer benchmark

questions.prompt: Is there a defect in how this code hashes and plans chunk uploads on its hot path (allocation, copying, or correctness of the chunking)? If so, mark the line(s) where it is; otherwise answer that there is none.
index_file is called for a 10 GiB file with a 64 KiB chunk size and a single 8 MiB scratch block. Roughly how much memory does the call need on top of the scratch block?
choices: 10 GiB, because the whole file is read before it is split into chunks.
About 8 MiB per chunk, because every ChunkRef holds a copy of its block.
About 4 MiB, one 24-byte ChunkRef per 64 KiB chunk, so it grows with the number of chunks and not with the bytes read.
Nothing, because the refs vector is not reserved and shrinks as chunks are consumed.

questions.prompt: In BM_Split the output vector is reserved once and out.clear() is called at the start of every iteration. What does this accomplish?
choices: It keeps the vector's capacity, so the timed loop measures hashing and pushing refs rather than reallocation and page faults on a fresh buffer.
It forces the compiler to evaluate indexer.split instead of optimising it away.
It frees the memory between iterations so peak usage stays low.

questions.prompt: A caller uploads a file containing the same 4 KiB block 1,000 times, and the remote store has none of its chunks. What does chunks_to_upload return?
choices: Indexes of all 1,000 chunks, because already_remote contains none of them.
An empty list, because identical chunks are treated as already uploaded.
Only the index of the first occurrence, because the local queued set filters the repeats.
The indexes of every second chunk, because of the queued.reserve call.
